item.title: No forced religious activities or fundraising contributions in schools – Voresara
item.description: Students and teachers should not be forced to participate in religious activities that go against their beliefs, while schools will be required to properly account for money collected from parents under the Education Act 2026. Principal Education Officer Amini Voresara highlighted these requirements during the Ministry of Representatives' public consultation at the Lami Parish Catholic Hall.
item.content:encoded:
Students and teachers should not be forced to participate in religious activities that go against their beliefs, while schools will be required to properly account for money collected from parents under the Education Act 2026.

Principal Education Officer Amini Voresara highlighted these requirements during the Ministry of Representatives' public consultation at the Lami Parish Catholic Hall.

Voresara says schools must respect the religious beliefs of all students and teachers, regardless of the school's religious affiliation.

He says even in faith-based schools, students and teachers who follow a different religion should not be required to participate in religious activities against their beliefs.

Voresara cites Catholic schools as an example, saying teachers who are not Catholic should not be forced to attend religious activities against their wishes.

He says the same principle applies to students from different religious backgrounds .

Voresara stresses that schools must respect individual beliefs and ensure everyone is treated fairly.

Meanwhile, the Principal Education Officer says schools will also be required to properly account for money collected from parents, including building and sports levies.

He says school management teams and heads of schools must ensure that all money collected is properly recorded and used for its intended purpose.

Voresara says schools cannot introduce levies without approval, as requests for building and sports levies must go through the Permanent Secretary for Education.

He says money collected from parents for a building project must be used for that project and cannot be diverted to social activities or other purposes.

Voresara stresses that school management teams and heads of schools will be held accountable if funds are misused.

He says all schools, including boarding schools, will also be required to prepare annual financial reports and submit them to the Ministry of Education.

Voresara says concerns have been raised about schools collecting money from parents without proper approval or accountability.

He says some schools have collected funds several times a year without obtaining the necessary approval.

The Principal Education Officer also stresses that parents and guardians cannot be forced to contribute to school fundraising activities.

He says all fundraising contributions must be voluntary, even when fundraising activities have been approved.

Voresara adds that parents who choose not to contribute must not be treated unfairly.

He says the new requirements aim to protect individual rights, strengthen financial accountability and ensure schools treat students, teachers and parents fairly.

The Education Act 2026 is expected to come into effect on 1 January 2027.

item.title: Cabinet endorses National Action Plan to prevent violence against children
item.description: The National Action Plan to Prevent Violence Against Children 2026-2031 has been endorsed by Cabinet, with the Government expected to launch the plan this month as part of efforts to strengthen child protection across Fiji. This has been revealed by Minister for Women, Children, Social Protection and Cohesion Sashi Kiran after MP Alipate Tuicolo questioned what actions are being taken by the Minis
item.content:encoded:
The National Action Plan to Prevent Violence Against Children 2026-2031 has been endorsed by Cabinet, with the Government expected to launch the plan this month as part of efforts to strengthen child protection across Fiji.

This has been revealed by Minister for Women, Children, Social Protection and Cohesion Sashi Kiran after MP Alipate Tuicolo questioned what actions are being taken by the Ministry to prevent violence against children.

She says the plan will provide a coordinated national framework to strengthen the prevention of and response to violence against children.

She says the Department of Children has completed the regulations for the Child Care and Protection Act 2024 and the Child Justice Act 2024, which are now at the final stage of legal vetting.

Kiran says regulations have also been developed for the Sexual Offenders Register, established under the Registration of Sex Offenders Act 2021, which has yet to become operational.

Kiran says the Ministry is also continuing the nationwide rollout of the National Child Safeguarding Policy, launched in October 2025 which promotes shared responsibility for child safeguarding across the public and private sectors , particularly organisations and institutions that work with children or provide services to them.

This includes continuous safeguarding training for personnel, faster regulation of safeguarding complaints and increased awareness programmes.

She says many organisations, including sporting bodies, are already actively implementing the policy.

Kiran says the Ministry has also revived the National Coordinating Committee on Children to ensure child protection efforts are coordinated and monitored across different sectors.

She says the Ministry continues to work with the Fiji Police Force, schools, health services, civil society organisations and other stakeholders to identify children at risk and ensure those experiencing violence, abuse, neglect or exploitation receive timely assistance.

This includes assessment, counselling, safe placement and other necessary interventions.

Kiran also highlighted the National Child Helpline 1325, which provides a free, confidential 24-hour service for children and adults across Fiji.

The Minister also highlights they have launched the Bebo Parenting App, a free digital resource providing guidance to parents and caregivers from pregnancy until their child reaches six years of age.

She says the helpline allows children to seek counselling, protection or emergency intervention, while also enabling neighbours, relatives and teachers to report suspected cases of abuse early.

Kiran says these initiatives demonstrate the Ministry's commitment to strengthening Fiji's child protection systems through legal reforms, safeguarding policies, positive parenting and coordinated support services.

However, she stresses that protecting children cannot be left to Government alone stressing, parents and guardians must actively supervise their children, including their digital activities, while maintaining open communication so children feel safe to speak up when something goes wrong.

Kiran says child protection is a collective responsibility that must extend to homes, schools, villages and settlements.

She also acknowledged UNICEF Pacific for its support in developing the National Action Plan to Prevent Violence Against Children 2026-2031.

Kiran also urged families to remain vigilant and protect their children, particularly during the current dry period, as she wished Fijians a joyous Diwali and called on everyone to collectively ensure that every child is protected from violence.

item.title: Parkinson urges Leadership Fiji graduates and alumni to make a difference in their communities
item.description: As 25 members of the Leadership Fiji 2026 programme celebrate their graduation, Leadership Fiji founder and Chair William Parkinson is urging them to take responsibility for shaping the country's future and making a difference in their communities. Speaking at the graduation and the organisation's 25th anniversary celebration, Parkinson says leadership is not about holding a position, but about ta
item.content:encoded:
As 25 members of the Leadership Fiji 2026 programme celebrate their graduation, Leadership Fiji founder and Chair William Parkinson is urging them to take responsibility for shaping the country's future and making a difference in their communities.

Speaking at the graduation and the organisation's 25th anniversary celebration, Parkinson says leadership is not about holding a position, but about taking action and making a difference every day.

He says the 25 graduates are now part of a growing network of 662 people who have completed Leadership Fiji's core programme over the past 25 years.

Parkinson says the organisation is now looking towards generational change, with its graduates expected to play a greater role in taking Fiji forward.

He believes leadership is not only about having the courage to stand up and lead, but also knowing when to step aside and allow the next generation to take responsibility.

Reflecting on the organisation's beginnings, Parkinson says Leadership Fiji was established following the political unrest of 2000, when many people were concerned about the country's future.

He says the events of that year highlighted the need to develop leaders who understood the importance of building a modern, multiracial and multireligious Fiji.

Parkinson says a meeting with representatives of Leadership Victoria in Melbourne helped inspire the establishment of Leadership Fiji, with a vision to prepare people who could lead the country towards a better future.

He says 25 years later, the organisation continues to invest in developing leaders who can bring positive change to their workplaces, communities and the country.

Parkinson also reminds the graduates that leadership must be guided by values rather than political divisions, particularly at a time when misinformation and political uncertainty are affecting societies around the world.

He encourages the graduates to carry Leadership Fiji's values of leadership, excellence, adaptability, diversity, empowerment, respect and service as they take on new responsibilities and continue their fellowship projects.

FM96 News Editor, Alipate Narawa was part of the 26 graduates this year.

Meanwhile, Leadership Fiji has also launched its Youth Leadership and Career Pathway Programme this year, attracting around 225 participants from across the country.

The organisation plans to expand the programme next year and is also working towards establishing a permanent leadership centre, with the aim of creating a regional hub for leadership training in the Pacific.
